title: The January 1933 Victor sessions and how the music was assembled
summary: DeMichael lists the many titles recorded days after Armstrong's return; Randolph says some were head-arranged in the studio and he had prepared Swing You Cats and High Society.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Well, in the -- to go back to '33, Louis came back to Chicago, according to what I've seen, in January of '33, he had come back from England.
Uh-huh.
And the band's first recording session took place just a few days after he arrived back.
Uh-huh.
And -- I have the records here -- he recorded, let's see, he recorded 'Got The World On A String', 'Got A Right To Sing The Blues'.
Yeah.
'Hustling and Bustling for Baby', 'Sitting In The Dark', 'High Society' --
'High Society'.

'He's A Son Of The South', and then the next day, 'Some Sweet Day', 'Basin Street Blues', 'Honey Do'. And the day after that, 'Snowball', 'Mahogany Hall Stomp' and 'Swing You Cats.' Which is a lot of music.
Yes.
And the band hadn't been together, and on the road.
Uh-huh.
Did you write all that music right from that -- did Louis pick the tunes? Or did you have some arrangements that you just brought in, that you had already written?
Yeah, well, I had --
How did you get all that music together?
Well, I had -- I thought there was another one in there, that other -- what's the name of that, Carpenters Dunlap Cotton, this number should have been in that, too.
Oh, 'You Can Depend On Me'?
'You Can Depend On Me'.
You had done that in '31, or '32.
Oh, we did that -- oh.
About a year before.
Oh, maybe so, maybe we did do that in -- Okay
That was for and this session, for January '33, was for Victor.
Victor, oh, uh-huh.
By the way, where were those studios? Do you recall?
Now, Merchandise Mart I remember, Victor was -- we were in the Merchandise Mart.
Uh-huh.
But the other studios, I don't recall where they was.
Someplace downtown.
Downtown, yes, someplace down there.
It's not important. I was just curious.

Well, now, getting back to your question, no, some of those things we would get together on that stuff right there in the studio, because "Snowball" -- I think that's Hoagy Carmichael's number, isn't it?
I believe so.
Yeah. I remember that, Hoagy Carmichael, yes. We would get together and talk over the -- do one of those talk -- did you ever do one of those talked arrangements things?
Yeah, the head arrangements.
Yeah. That's what we did. Did some of those, uh-huh.

But had you prepared any music previous to hearing from Louis, before you heard from Louis, did you have some arrangements, and then when the recording -- you said, well, look, I've got this arrangement we can do, whatever it is?
Well, only the -- I know the Swing You Cats, I had that.
Yeah.
And I had -- and then, now, 'High Society', we had played that down in Suburban Garden.
